title: Measure the instrument
subtitle: A result is only as good as the proof that the measurement measured the thing
lede: Every performance programme I have run has produced at least one result that was really a property of the measurement. A profiler that serialised the copy engine it was observing. A test suite that passed a thousand trials against the wrong code. A benchmark whose baseline had a stall bug. A headline that beat a weak comparison. I treat the instrument as part of the experiment, and I do not act on a number until I know what the instrument did to it. Every instrumented run has an uninstrumented control. Every evaluation set is frozen before the model sees it and carries known-answer controls that can catch the team as readily as the model.
quote: The instinct to protect is the instinct to believe a number that agrees with you.
evidence: Performance benchmarking methodology: an uninstrumented control for every instrumented run, the strongest baseline I could build, and a profiler verdict retracted when the profiler caused the serialisation.
Numerical reproducibility and bitwise validation: parity gates bitwise only where the reference agrees with itself across two runs, judged within its own spread elsewhere.
Evaluation design for ML: evaluation sets frozen before the model sees them, with known-answer controls, and a classical retriever that tied the model published as the result.
author: Corey James
